forms.definition: separating something into parts
forms.example: The division of the land took many years.
forms.note: division is also maths (12 ÷ 3) and a part of a company.

syn.note: Moving things or people apart.
A break into parts; a little informal.

forms.definition: to separate something into two or more parts
forms.example: Divide the class into four groups.

syn.note: The easiest word; also used for sharing money.
To move things apart.
To give a part to each person.
To make parts with a knife.

forms.definition: separated into parts
forms.example: The road is divided into two lanes.

syn.note: Broken into parts.
Kept apart.

forms.definition: able to be shared into equal parts
forms.example: Ten is divisible by two.

forms.definition: causing people to disagree strongly
forms.example: Money became a divisive topic in the family.
forms.note: Belongs to divide = make people disagree, not separating into parts.

people.definition: something that separates a space into parts
people.example: A wooden divider separates the two desks.

context.text: Grandma divided the big melon into eight pieces. Everyone was happy with the division, even my little brother.

reviewer_note: divisive (disagreement) as other_meaning; -ible is not in the affix table.

forms.definition: the legal end of a marriage
forms.example: Their divorce was finalised last spring.

syn.note: Living apart; it is not always a legal end.
The end of any relationship.

ant.note: The ceremony where two people marry.

forms.definition: to end a marriage by law
forms.example: They divorced after ten years together.

syn.note: To start living apart.
To go away from a partner.

forms.definition: no longer married because of a legal end
forms.example: Her parents are divorced.

syn.note: Living apart but maybe still married.

people.definition: a person whose marriage has legally ended
people.example: She became a divorcee at forty.

context.text: Their divorce was difficult for the children. Now the parents are divorced, but they still have dinner together on holidays.

reviewer_note: Spelling: finalised (British) / finalized (American) in the corpus example.

forms.definition: the legal end of a marriage
forms.example: They talked to a lawyer about divorce.

syn.note: Living apart; it is not always a legal end.

forms.definition: to end a marriage by law
forms.example: They decided to divorce last year.

syn.note: To start living apart.

forms.definition: no longer married to your husband or wife by law
forms.example: My parents are divorced but remain friends.

syn.note: Living apart but maybe still married.
Not married now, for any reason.

people.definition: a person whose marriage has legally ended
people.example: My aunt is a divorcee with two sons.

context.text: Aziz is divorced and lives with his son. The divorce happened five years ago, but the family is still close.

reviewer_note: Participle adjective headword; divorce noun/verb as source forms.

forms.definition: the feeling that everything is turning around you
forms.example: The medicine can cause dizziness.

syn.note: The same feeling; less common.
A medical word, often a fear of high places.

forms.definition: feeling that everything is spinning and you may fall
forms.example: I felt dizzy after the long bus ride.

syn.note: The same feeling; also means silly and excited.
Not able to stand or walk well.
Feeling weak, as if you will fall down.

forms.definition: making you feel that everything is spinning
forms.example: We looked down from a dizzying height.

syn.note: So high, fast or beautiful that it surprises you.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you feel unsteady
forms.example: He stood up dizzily after the game.

syn.note: In the same way; less common.

context.text: The summer heat in Termez made me feel dizzy. The doctor said the dizziness came from not drinking enough water.

reviewer_note: verb dizzy (to make dizzy) is rare; only the participle dizzying is shown.

particle_note: Separable: do up your coat / do your coat up; with a pronoun only do it up.

relations.note: The same action; a little more formal.
Only for clothes or bags with a zip (US: zipper).
To open buttons, zips or knots.

context.text: It is very cold outside, so do up your coat. My little sister cannot do her buttons up yet, so I help her.

reviewer_note: British do up = repair/decorate a house is a different meaning, not shown.

forms.definition: something boring or annoying
forms.example: Waiting for the bus is such a drag.
forms.note: Belongs to drag = boring thing (informal), not pulling something.

forms.definition: to pull something heavy along the ground
forms.example: He dragged the heavy box into the kitchen.

syn.note: The easiest word; drag means pulling with effort.
To pull something very heavy.
To pull a car or boat with a rope.

ant.note: To move something away from you.

context.text: The suitcase was too heavy to carry. So I dragged it all the way from the station to the hotel.

reviewer_note: drag (computer: drag and drop) is the same pulling meaning. dragon is not family.

forms.definition: the system that carries water away from a place
forms.example: The city needs better drainage after heavy rain.

forms.definition: to make liquid flow away; to use up energy
forms.example: Drain the pasta before you add the sauce.

syn.note: To take everything out of a container.
To make someone very tired.
To slowly take away energy or strength.

ant.note: To put liquid into something until it is full.

forms.definition: very tired, with no energy left
forms.example: I felt drained after the long exam.

syn.note: Extremely tired.
The easiest word; less strong.

ant.note: Rested and full of energy again.

forms.definition: making you very tired
forms.example: Looking after a new baby is draining.

syn.note: Very tiring.
Making you tired; less strong.

people.definition: a pipe or hole that takes dirty water away
people.example: Hair blocked the drain in the shower.

context.text: After washing the rice, drain the water carefully. Cooking plov for forty guests left my mother completely drained.

reviewer_note: Corpus covers both meanings (liquid + energy); one map. drain (pipe) as thing per Rule 8; -age not in affix table.

forms.definition: a small creature in fairy tales, or a very small person
forms.example: The story has seven dwarfs and a princess.
forms.note: Plural dwarfs (also dwarves in fantasy books). Calling a real person a dwarf can be offensive.

syn.note: A small old man in fairy tales who lives under the ground.
A small magic creature with pointed ears.

ant.note: A very big creature or person.

forms.definition: to make something look very small next to it
forms.example: The new tower dwarfs the old houses around it.

syn.note: To be much bigger or more important than something.

forms.note: dwarf before a noun (dwarf trees) is the noun used like an adjective; dwarfish is rare.

context.text: In the fantasy film, a brave dwarf saves the village. Next to the huge dragon, he is dwarfed, but he does not run away.

reviewer_note: Sensitive word: offensive for real people, noted on the entry.

forms.definition: a substance used to change the colour of hair, cloth or food
forms.example: She bought blue dye for her hair.
forms.note: Do not mix up with die (stop living), which sounds the same.

syn.note: A substance that gives colour, often a powder.
A light colour added to something.
A coloured liquid you put on a surface.

forms.definition: to change the colour of something with a special liquid
forms.example: My grandmother dyes wool with onion skins.

syn.note: To give something a colour. British spelling: colour.
To add a light colour.

ant.note: To make something lighter or white with chemicals.

forms.definition: having a colour that was added
forms.example: He has dyed black hair.

syn.note: With colour added. British spelling: coloured.

ant.note: As it was, with nothing added.

people.definition: a person whose job is changing the colour of cloth
people.example: The dyer in Margilan uses old methods for silk.

context.text: In Margilan, workers make natural dye from plants. The dyed silk is then woven into bright scarves.

reviewer_note: die/dye homophone and dyeing spelling noted.

forms.definition: a family of rulers who rule a country for many years
forms.example: The Timurid dynasty built many beautiful buildings.

syn.note: A series of people from the same family.
The easiest word; not always rulers.
The time when one king or queen rules.

forms.definition: connected with a family of rulers
forms.example: The country had a long dynastic history.

context.text: The Timurid dynasty ruled Central Asia for more than a hundred years. Its dynastic capital, Samarkand, became famous for science and art.
